questions.prompt: A hospital uses a fecal transplant to treat a patient's recurring C. difficile infection. Which concept from Module 18 best explains why it works?

options.text: The transplant raises the colon's pH to 7.35, killing C. diff
The transplant contains antibiotics that kill C. difficile directly
The transplant turns C. difficile into a harmless mutualist
Restoring diverse normal flora brings back microbial antagonism

questions.explanation: Slides: fecal transplants restore beneficial microbiota; more diverse flora outcompete pathogens.

questions.prompt: A researcher isolates a new virus from patients but can't grow it outside human cells and can't ethically infect volunteers. Which TWO limitations of Koch's postulates apply?

options.text: It is endemic in the region, and it is also sporadic
It has several possible causes, and it is non-communicable
It can't be pure-cultured, and testing on humans would be unethical
It is a latent infection, and it is also subclinical

questions.explanation: These are the same limitations that have kept Koch's postulates from being completed for HIV and AIDS.

questions.prompt: Lyme disease is infectious but, per the slides, non-communicable. Which statement must therefore be true?

options.text: Not all infectious diseases are communicable
Lyme disease is caused by normal flora
Lyme disease is contagious
All non-communicable diseases are non-infectious

questions.explanation: All communicable diseases are infectious, but not all infectious diseases are communicable (tetanus, Lyme).

questions.prompt: A patient's infection follows the disease curve. Which statement is FALSE?

options.text: A patient who feels fine during convalescence has no microbes left.
Stopping antibiotics early can leave the most resistant microbes behind.
Incubation has microbes but no signs or symptoms.
Prodromal symptoms are mild, like 'I'm coming down with something.'
The period of illness matches exponential (log) growth of the pathogen.

questions.explanation: During convalescence the curve hasn't yet reached zero.

questions.prompt: If a disease's incidence stays constant but patients start living much longer with it (no cure), what happens to prevalence?

options.text: It rises, because fewer cases leave while new ones keep coming
It falls, because incidence is staying exactly the same
It becomes equal to incidence once deaths stop entirely
It stays the same, because incidence isn't changing at all

questions.explanation: Prevalence = existing + new cases; fewer deaths means cases accumulate.

questions.prompt: Which scenario describes a SPORADIC disease becoming an EPIDEMIC?

options.text: A brand-new flu strain spreads to every continent within a few short months
A town rarely sees cholera; then floodwater taints wells and dozens fall ill in a week
Diabetes rates in a state rise slowly and steadily over the course of a decade
The common cold circulates all year in a large city, with someone always sick

questions.explanation: Sporadic = occasional; epidemic = many cases in an area in a short time.

questions.prompt: Which pairing of infection type and example is INCORRECT?

options.text: Latent — herpes fever blisters
Local — abscessed tooth
Subclinical — measles
Acute — food poisoning

questions.explanation: Measles is systemic with obvious spots; the lecture's subclinical example is hepatitis A.

questions.prompt: Why might normal-flora S. aureus cause a wound infection after surgery even though it was harmless before?

options.text: Surgery converts S. aureus into S. epidermidis, which then infects the cut
It's an opportunistic pathogen introduced to a new site beneath the skin
S. aureus is a true pathogen that always causes disease wherever it lives
Surgery kills all skin bacteria, so any S. aureus must be a new arrival

questions.explanation: On unbroken skin S. aureus is commensal; through a cut, it reaches tissue where it causes disease.

questions.prompt: An elderly patient on chemotherapy develops pneumonia caused by a normally harmless microbe. Which combination of terms fits best?

options.text: Passive carrier, latent infection, endemic disease in the ward
Compromised host, predisposing factors, opportunistic pathogen
Healthy host, true pathogen, herd immunity from vaccination
Commensal relationship, subclinical infection, pandemic spread

questions.explanation: Age and immunosuppressive therapy weaken defenses so opportunists can cause disease.

questions.prompt: Which observation best supports the idea that normal flora protect against Salmonella?

options.text: Salmonella can only grow on the skin, where E. coli is never found
Lactobacillus raises the intestinal pH so that Salmonella can't grow
S. epidermidis lives in the colon and crowds out Salmonella there
E. coli in the intestine releases bacteriocins that inhibit Salmonella

questions.explanation: Bacteriocins are one of the three antagonism mechanisms.

questions.prompt: A disease has a long incubation period with no symptoms, yet the patient can spread it. Which concept explains this?

options.text: The disease must be latent
The disease is non-communicable
The patient is a passive carrier who is not infected
The patient is an active carrier during incubation

questions.explanation: Textbook: active carriers can transmit during incubation, before signs and symptoms appear.

questions.prompt: Sepsis differs from bacteremia because sepsis is:

options.text: A local infection confined to one organ that never reaches the blood
Toxins present in the blood with no bacteria anywhere in the body
An extreme immune reaction to pathogens or toxins that can cause shock
Simply the presence of bacteria in the blood, with or without symptoms

questions.explanation: Bacteremia is a condition (bacteria in blood); sepsis is the dangerous body-wide reaction.

questions.prompt: A baby born by C-section initially lacks large numbers of which normal flora, according to the lecture's acquisition routes?

options.text: Lactobacillus acidophilus
Staphylococcus epidermidis
Staphylococcus aureus
Escherichia coli

questions.explanation: L. acidophilus is acquired by passing through the vaginal canal; slides note C-section babies meet different microbes.

questions.prompt: Using the three types of symbiosis, explain how E. coli can be mutualistic in one person's colon and cause disease in another person's bladder.
questions.explanation: In the colon E. coli is mutualistic (+/+): it gets a moist, food-rich home and makes vitamin K and bacteriocins. In the urinary tract it is an opportunistic pathogen acting parasitically (+/−), causing a UTI. Location changes the relationship.

questions.prompt: Explain herd immunity and why falling vaccination rates have led to more measles cases.
questions.explanation: Herd immunity is immunity in most of a population (mainly from vaccination); the pathogen can't find enough susceptible hosts, protecting those who aren't immune. When fewer people vaccinate, there are more susceptible hosts, so measles (highly contagious) can spread again and its incidence rises.
